doc.title: Lou Pallo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Guitar collection and working at The New York Times
summary: Pallo keeps eight to ten guitars, and recalls three years as a production manager for The New York Times before returning to music.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: How many guitars do you own now?

Ooh. What do I have. Not that many. Not many because I like to play them all so every week I change and I’ll bring each one in so I can play them. So I have approximately eight, nine, ten, somewhere around there. I have given a lot to my son that I don’t use.
That’s neat. At least your guitars don’t get so lonely, they don’t get touched.

Right. Never get lonely. I was always told that if you have an instrument you should play it and not just leave it in the case because then the neck tends to go on you after a while and so forth. You have to play it. You have to play all the instruments so I like to change.
Have you always made a living as a musician?
Not always but I would say the majority of my life, yes, the majority.
And even when you weren’t you were probably playing.
I was still playing on weekends.

Right. I just — when I was first married I took a job, I was a production manager with The New York Times and it was in New Jersey, they had a subsidiary. And I did that for about three years and playing weekends and then the headaches started coming because of working so many hours as a production manager and the pressure, I said I’m going back to music. I went back into music and stayed in music since then.
